Check if the game ends 2.6 Permit refusal 3 Effects 3.1 Surveyor (white fence) 3.2 Agent (purple arrow) 3.3 Landscaper (green trees) 3.4 Pool manufacturer (blue pool) 3.5 Temp agency (orange construction) 3.6 Bis (red mailbox) 4 City plans 5 Scoring 6 Variants 7 Advanced variant 7.1 Advanced city plans 8 Expert rules 9 Board: Ice cream truck 9.1 Scoring 9.2 City plans 10 Board: Christmas lights 10.1 Scoring 10.2 City plans 11 Board: Easter eggs 11.1 Scoring 11.2 City plans Setup Each player has their personal game sheet . The top half of the sheet contains the three streets , each divided into several houses . The bottom half of the sheet is for scoring. Your game sheet is for your own use only. Players never write on other players' sheets. In every game, there are 3 shared city plans , numbered no.1 (blue), no.2 (yellow), and no.3 (red). These are goals that players may compete for points. In addition, there is a deck of 81 construction cards . Each construction card has a number (1-15) on the front face, and an effect (6 possible effects) on the back face. Certain numbers and effects are more common than others; see #Construction card breakdown for a full table. Game overview The following describes the basic game. See #Variants for game variants that may change some aspects of the game. The game is divided into turns. Every turn, all players play simultaneously. The game continues until one player triggers the end of the game. Each turn follows these steps: 1. New construction cards are revealed. There will be 3 number/effect pairs. 2. Choose one of the number/effect pairs, and write in the number on one of your empty houses. 3. Optionally, use the effect on your chosen pair. 4. You may complete any city plan. 5. All players' choices are revealed. Check if the game ends. 1. New construction cards are revealed The construction cards are divided into 3 stacks of 27 cards each, initially showing the number side. Every turn, the top card is flipped over, turning it into the effect side while revealing the next number side. Note: The number side of each card also shows its effect side on the corners. Because of how the cards are flipped, this means the effects on the corners are exactly the effects you'll see next turn. If the decks run out, the top card of each discard pile (showing the effect sides) is kept, and all other cards are reshuffled to make new piles. 2. Choose a number/effect pair and write its number Choose one of the three available number/effect pairs. Then choose one of your empty houses, and write in the number in that house. Your house numbers must follow this rule: house numbers on a street must be strictly increasing from left to right . Duplicates are not allowed. However, gaps are allowed, including gaps that wouldn't be able to be filled with numbers. Also, numbers do not have to be consecutive; e.g. it is legal to put a 10 to the right of a 7. You must write in the number. It is not legal to choose a number/action pair and then not write in the number. If any of the numbers among the number/effect pairs can be written, you must choose a number/action pair. If you cannot, you will have to take a permit refusal . (See #Permit refusal below.) 3. [Rating: 2/10] Don't like the player pencil-and-paper genre, because cheating and honest mistakes are likely (and it's not feasible to check what your opponents are doing). This one's "busier" than most.

[Rating: 2/10] I do find something quite appealing about the puzzle here and especially about a game involving drawing on a piece of paper, which at least takes things to a different level of tactility than a player board.  All that said, this is more puzzle than game (the only real interaction is that any player having three impossible placements will immediately end the game, which is unsatisfying for everybody involved) and I would really rather prefer something where my opponents are able to do things to make me think.
